records.label: 100KGP discovery cases with RNU4-2 variants in n.62-70 and n.73-79
records.segregation: 37 of 47 de novo; 10 unknown inheritance; one parent (mother of G38) mosaic for n.65A>G
quotes: Of the 47 rare allele instances in the regions, which we observed in 47 cases, 37 were determined to be de novo on the basis of genotype calls in the respective parents, while 10 had unknown inheritance because of missing genotypes from one or both of the corresponding parents (Fig. 1d,e).
Of these 46 cases, 91% had the ID term, 91% had ‘Neurodevelopmental delay’ and 61% had ‘Motor delay’, broadly in line with general term frequencies across ID cases (Fig. 2a).

including ‘Microcephaly’ in 57% (versus 18% in other NDA-coded cases, Bonferroni-adjusted P = 3.23 × 10−7), ‘Drooling’ in 13% (versus 1%, P = 6.93 × 10−4), ‘Proportionate short stature’ in 28% (versus 7%, P = 7.60 × 10−4), ‘Generalized hypotonia’ in 39% (versus 13%, P = 8.08 × 10−4), ‘Seizure’ in 52%

records.label: Replication probands (NBR, 100KGP Pilot, GMS)
records.ancestry: UK; one NBR pedigree from Belgium

variants.as_reported: rare variant within the two regions of interest (n.62–70 and n.73–79)

records.segregation: 19 of 26 de novo; 6 unknown; one inherited n.76C>T from an affected mother
quotes: Across these three collections, we identified a further 27 probands with a rare variant within the two regions of interest, of whom 25 were NDA coded, one was coded with ‘Abnormal brain morphology’ terms such that NDA could be inferred, and one was unaffected (Fig. 1e).

In total, 19 of the 26 affected probands acquired the variant de novo, six acquired the variant with inheritance that was unknown because of a lack of parental genotype data and one case inherited variant n.76C>T from an affected mother.

This includes photographs showing recognizable facial features for this novel disorder

records.label: Remaining 66 individuals with RNU4-2 critical-region variants without detailed phenotyping
records.segregation: Most de novo (86 of 115 with both parents sequenced overall); n.77_78insT in two affected siblings; n.65A>G apparently mosaic in mother
quotes: In total, we identified 115 individuals with variants across this region, including 61 individuals in GEL (60 probands and one more sibling) and 54 from extra cohorts

Most of the 115 individuals have the initial n.64_65insT variant (n = 89; 77.4%). Five of the 11 extra variants are also single base insertions, including n.77_78insT (GRCh38:chr. 12: 120291826:T:TA), which is seen in six individuals, two of whom are affected siblings.
In one individual the n.65A>G variant appeared to be mosaic in the mother (54 reference and eight alternate reads) and in another an SNV was maternally inherited (n.76C>T).

notes.statement: Chen et al. (2024) characterized the RNU4-2 syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder as moderate to severe global developmental delay and intellectual disability in all individuals, with delayed ambulation, mostly absent speech, microcephaly, short stature, hypotonia, seizures, brain MRI abnormalities, and distinctive facial features.
quotes: we find the RNU4-2 syndromic NDD to be characterized by moderate to severe global developmental delay (four children with SNVs with moderate delay) and intellectual disability in all individuals.

Associated growth and neurodevelopmental phenotypes present in more than or equal to 75% of individuals include short stature, microcephaly (mostly congenital), speech abnormalities (mostly non-verbal), hypotonia and seizures.

notes.statement: Chen et al. (2024) identified heterozygous variants in an 18-bp critical region of RNU4-2 (nucleotides 62-79) in 115 individuals with NDD; 77.4% carried the recurrent n.64_65insT insertion. In 54 individuals in whom it could be determined, the de novo variants were all on the maternal allele.
quotes: we identify heterozygous variants in 115 individuals with NDD. Most individuals (77.4%) have the same highly recurrent single base insertion (n.64_65insT). In 54 individuals in whom it could be determined, the de novo variants were all on the maternal allele.

notes.statement: Chen et al. (2024) found that the n.64_65insT variant arose de novo in 38 GEL probands and was absent from 3,408 diagnosed NDD probands, 21,817 non-NDD probands, 33,122 unaffected individuals, gnomAD v4.0, and All of Us; single base insertions in the critical region were strongly enriched in undiagnosed NDD probands versus UK Biobank (OR 1,531).
quotes: The n.64_65insT variant was not found in any of 3,408 NDD probands with an existing genetic diagnosis, 21,817 probands with non-NDD phenotypes or 33,122 unaffected individuals.

54 out of 8,841 (0.61%) GEL undiagnosed NDD probands (55 out of 10,388 individuals) have single base insertions compared to two out of 490,132 individuals in the UK Biobank (OR = 1,531; 95% confidence interval (CI): 404–16,384; Fisher’s P = 3.3 × 10−92).

notes.statement: Chen et al. (2024) observed that children with SNVs in the critical region had fewer reports of severe global developmental delay than those with single base insertions (0 of 4 vs 34 of 40), suggesting a milder phenotype, though based on only 4 fully phenotyped individuals.
quotes: In comparison to the single base insertions, children with SNVs had fewer reports of severe global developmental delay (zero out of four versus 34 out of 40, Fisher’s P = 0.0015).
our initial data suggest these SNVs may result in a milder phenotype. However, given this observation is based on only four fully phenotyped individuals, it needs to be confirmed in larger cohorts.

notes.statement: Chen et al. (2024) performed blood RNA-seq in 5 individuals with RNU4-2 variants and found increased use of unannotated 5-prime splice sites compared with controls, with a shift away from consensus at the +3, +4, and +5 positions that pair with U6 ACAGAGA, suggesting that the variants disrupt accurate 5-prime splice-site recognition during spliceosome activation.
quotes: the most pronounced difference was observed for abnormal splicing events corresponding to increased use of unannotated 5′ splice sites (mean 8.8 events in individuals with RNU4-2 variants compared with 0.7 in both 378 unmatched controls and ten controls matched on genetic ancestry, sex and age at consent

These three positions of the 5′ splice site (+3, +4 and +5), which shift away from consensus in individuals with RNU4-2 variants, pair directly with the U6 ACAGAGA region during spliceosome activation

notes.statement: Chen et al. (2024) noted that the 18-bp critical region maps to the T-loop (quasi-pseudoknot) and stem III of the U4/U6 duplex, which are loaded into the BRR2 helicase and are thought to stabilize U4/U6 pairing and position U6 ACAGAGA to receive the 5-prime splice site.
quotes: The highly recurrent n.64_65insT variant is within a previously described ‘quasi pseudoknot’, or T-loop, structure (Fig. 1d). The region spanning nucleotides 76 to 78, where the recurrent n.77_78insT variant resides, is involved in base pairing with U6 in stem III

notes.statement: Chen et al. (2024) showed that RNU4-2 is expressed at consistently higher levels than its homolog RNU4-1 in human prefrontal cortex across development and has greater chromatin accessibility in prenatal cortex, supporting RNU4-2 as the main U4 transcript in the brain.
quotes: The expression of RNU4-1 and RNU4-2 is tightly correlated (Supplementary Fig. 5), however, RNU4-2 is consistently expressed at a significantly higher level than RNU4-1 (Fig. 5a).
Overall, these data support the role of RNU4-2 as the main U4 transcript in the brain.

notes.statement: Chen et al. (2024) estimated that variants in the 18-bp critical region of RNU4-2 explain about 0.4% of all individuals with NDD; variants were found in 0.68% of undiagnosed NDD probands in GEL versus 0.008% of UK Biobank individuals, and at a much lower rate in autism cohorts (3 of 7,149).
quotes: we estimate that variants in RNU4-2 could explain 0.4% of all NDD (calculated as 60 from an effective cohort size of 14,735 (8,841 × 1/0.6)).

This is consistent with the much lower rate of RNU4-2 variants in cohorts recruited primarily for autism spectrum disorder (for example, three out of 7,149; 0.042% across the Simons Simplex Collection (SSC), SPARK and MSSNG).

notes.statement: Chen et al. (2024) found that RNU4-2 is not captured by exome sequencing; of 22 individuals with n.64_65insT who also had DDD exome data, none had a read supporting the variant, indicating very low sensitivity of exome sequencing for detection.
quotes: Of 1,755 individuals in both GEL and DDD, 22 have the n.64_65insT variant (1.3%). Two of the 22 individuals (9.1%) each have a single read at the variant position in the exome sequencing data from DDD, but in each case it is identical to the reference sequence.
These analyses suggest that although it is possible to identify individuals who may have variants in RNU4-2 through exome sequencing data, the sensitivity of this approach is very low.

notes.statement: Chen et al. (2024) tested 28 brain-expressed snRNA genes and found no other snRNA, or constrained subregion, significantly enriched for de novo or recessive variants in undiagnosed NDD probands, although power was low.
quotes: We did not find any other snRNAs, or constrained subregions of snRNAs, that were significantly enriched for either de novo variants or recessively inherited variants in NDD cases when compared with non-NDD probands.

notes.statement: Schot et al. (2024) mined 164 diagnostic whole genome sequencing trios from individuals with neurodevelopmental or multiple congenital anomaly disorders and identified a recurrent de novo RNU4-2 variant in a previously unexplained case, illustrating that re-analysis of a negative diagnostic genome for noncoding variants can solve cases.
quotes: Here we mined 164 whole genome sequencing (WGS) trios from individuals with neurodevelopmental or multiple congenital anomaly disorders that received diagnostic genomic investigations at our clinic.
This case illustrates the power of re-analysis to solve previously unexplained cases even when a diagnostic genome remains negative.

notes.statement: Greene et al. (2024) performed a rare-variant burden association analysis of 41,132 noncoding genes in 5,529 unrelated intellectual disability cases and 46,401 controls from the 100,000 Genomes Project and found that RNU4-2 had an extremely strong dominant association with ID (posterior probability of association approximately 1, log Bayes factor 55), far stronger than any other noncoding gene.
quotes: We identified an extremely strong dominant association between rare variants in RNU4-2 and the risk of ID (posterior probability of association (PPA) ≈ 1, log Bayes factor = 55).
The association was much stronger than that for any other noncoding gene (all other PPAs < 0.5).

notes.statement: Greene et al. (2024) found that the disease-associated RNU4-2 variants clustered in 2 contiguous regions (n.62-70 and n.73-79) in which no unaffected participants carried a rare variant, within a locus depleted of variation in gnomAD. The most common variant, n.64_65insT, occurred de novo in 33 different families. In total 73 unrelated cases were identified after replication in 3 additional collections.
quotes: Five additional variants within a few base pairs of the three variants with a PPP > 0.5 were also present exclusively in affected participants, forming two contiguous regions (n.62–70 and n.73–79) within which no unaffected participants had a rare variant.
The most common variant, n.64_65insT, was observed as a de novo mutation in 33 different families.
We replicated this finding in three collections, bringing the number of unrelated cases to 73.

notes.statement: Greene et al. (2024) observed n.76C>T de novo in 4 families but inherited from an affected mother in 1 and present once in gnomAD, suggesting it may cause a less severe phenotype in some cases than other variants, particularly n.64_65insT; n.76C>G was found in an individual without neurodevelopmental abnormality, suggesting some position-76 changes may have limited or benign effect.
quotes: While we observed this variant as a de novo mutation in four families, the inheritance in one family and the observation in gnomAD suggest that it may cause a less severe phenotype in some cases than the other variants we identified, particularly the predominant variant n.64_65insT.
Moreover, variant n.76C>G was observed in one case without NDA, further suggesting that certain mutations at nucleotide position 76 may have limited or benign effect.

notes.statement: Greene et al. (2024) found that RNU4-2 cases accounted for 0.50% (46 of 9,112) of neurodevelopmental abnormality-coded cases in the 100,000 Genomes Project, making it the most prevalent etiology there, and 0.38% (21 of 5,527) in the UK Genomic Medicine Service, second only to MECP2 (24 cases).
quotes: To assess the prevalence of this new disorder, we compared the number of NDA-coded RNU4-2 cases in the 100KGP (46 of 9,112 NDA-coded cases, 0.50%) with the number of solved cases with P or LP variants in other etiological genes for NDA.
In the GMS, RNU4-2 was the second most prevalent etiology for NDA (21 of 5,527 NDA-coded cases, 0.38%) after MECP2 (24 cases)

notes.statement: Greene et al. (2024) noted that the variant regions map to the U4-U6 quasi-pseudoknot and stem III interactions, and proposed that n.64_65insT could disrupt the G64(U4)-A47(U6) interaction supporting the quasi-pseudoknot, so that a delay in U4-U6 unwinding similar to that in WBP4 deficiency might be the underlying mechanism.
quotes: Analysis of published secondary structure data of the U4 snRNA revealed that one region maps to a quasi-pseudoknot interaction between U4 and U6 while the other maps to an interaction between U4 and U6 called stem III (Extended Data Fig. 1).

Given that the predominant variant, n.64_65insT, could disrupt the G64(U4)–A47(U6) interaction supporting the quasi-pseudoknot structure, a delay in U4–U6 unwinding activity similar to that observed in WBP4 deficiency might be the underlying etiological mechanism of this newly described syndrome.

notes.statement: Greene et al. (2024) noted that RNU4-2, which encodes the U4 snRNA component of the major spliceosome, is ubiquitously expressed across adult tissues in GTEx data.
quotes: Many components of the major spliceosome are ubiquitously expressed, including RNU4-2 (Extended Data Fig. 3).
